newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia PM says ringgit fall forcing import cuts.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia PM says ringgit fall forcing import cuts.

text.p: Malaysia will reduce imports and review plans for some large projects due to a sharp fall by the ringgit against the U.S. dollar, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Wednesday.

"We want to reduce imports because now imports cost a little bit more due to the value of the ringgit has come down. Therefore, for the time being we have to reduce imports," he was quoted as saying by the national Bernama news agency.
The Malaysian ringgit has fallen 11 percent in the past month to around 2.7750 to the dollar on Wednesday due to selling pressure from overseas.
Implementation of some big projects was being reviewed as a "temporary measure" to reduce imports, Mahathir was quoted as telling reporters after meeting a Bosnian delegation.
He said the projects to be reviewed were big in value but were not "mega-projects". Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim had said on Tuesday execution of some mega-projects would be postponed.
Bernama quoted Mahathir as saying in reply to a question that the projects would not be postponed but only reviewed to reduce certain imports.
"Now our imports cost is a little bit more because the value of the ringgit has come down. For the time being, we have got to reduce imports but we will go on with these projects", he said.

The Prime Minister said the government in most cases did not spend money on mega-projects as they were done by the private sector. "But even if it is done by the private sector, we still have to reduce imports," he said.
He once again lashed out against speculators for causing chaos in the country's currency. He also blamed some rich countries for the turmoil in the currency markets.
Mahathir said: "What annoyed me is this kind of activities is actually being supported by very rich countries, and these countries don't even help poor countries."

The prime minister has blamed "rogue speculators" for the chaos in Southeast Asian currencies. He has also named U.S. financier George Soros as mainly responsible for an attack on the region's currencies. Soros has denied involvement.

"When they see poor countries, they try to knock them on their heads and yet they talk about justice, about democracy -- what democracy is this when the rich can squeeze the poor?" he said when asked to comment on the current drop in the value of the ringgit.
Mahathir was quoted as saying that these countries did not care what they did to other people, and they thought that destroying the economy of developing countries was great fun.
"Of course they don't suffer. What do they care? They talk about human rights, poverty eradication and all that. They think this is great," he said.
"They do this for democracy, for freedom and for free trade. I'm not talking about anybody, you can make your guess," he said.

But, Mahathir said, the Malaysian currency's fall was only temporary and the government was doing its very best towards a "final solution" to the problem. "We'll recover," he said, without elaborating.
